rationale: Current wording retains paired crossing wefts around passive stakes; it remains distinct from coiling (092), plaiting (094), and wickerwork (095). CCI says twining uses passive vertical stakes and two active wefts, one passing to the front as the other passes behind; they go over/under each other (lines 205–207). Distinct from 092 coiling, 094 flat plaiting without warp/weft roles, and 095 wickerwork where wefts do not cross each other within a row.

Current wording retains all-active, same-size flat strips without separate stakes; distinct from twining and wickerwork. CCI says plaiting has no distinct warp/weft; all elements are active, often same size, and checkerwork runs over-one/under-one in both directions (lines 226–228). This distinguishes it from 093’s passive stakes and paired twining and 095’s rigid willow framework.

Current wording retains willow stakes and non-crossing wefts; distinct from paired crossing in twining and stake-free plaiting. CCI describes wickerwork as interworked willow branches and says wefts do not cross other wefts in a row (lines 229–231). That is distinct from paired crossing wefts in twining (093) and same-sized active strips in plaiting (094).

Current scratch-and-burr wording remains distinct from 067’s repaired burin-cut groove, thin curl and ink-holding cut. Met defines drypoint as scratching metal with a sharp stylus/needle, leaving scrapings (burr) on either side that hold ink (line 68). The scratch-and-burr mechanism is distinct from repaired 067 engraving, where a burin cuts a groove and removes a curl.

Current bead-like granules remain distinct from 068’s fine-wire filigree and from enamel partitions or niello inlay. Met describes granulation as creating relief with small metal spheres and says they are attached to the sheet (lines 139–140). This is distinct from filigree wirework (068) and the enamel/niello techniques in 098–100; Met also supports the ancient-Egyptian amulet zigzag example.

Current added metal-strip dividers form enamel cells; distinct from granulation (097), carved cells (099), and black niello inlay (100). Getty AAT 300053778 Note says cloisonné uses thin metal strips on a ground to form chambers for vitreous enamel pastes (line 20). Distinct from 097 granules, 099 cells carved into the base, and 100 black inlay in engraved lines.

Current carved-out enamel cells remain distinct from the added partitions in 098 and black inlay in 100. Getty AAT 300053777 Note says champlevé carves troughs/cells into metal, leaving raised outlines; enamel is placed in the cells, fired and polished (line 20). Distinct from 098 added metal-strip dividers and 100 black niello inlay.

Current engraved lines filled with black metallic composition remain distinct from vitreous enamel in 098–099. Source supports the black inlay; no distractor introduces a potentially over-specific copper/silver/sulfur formula. Getty AAT 300054022 Note defines niello as engraving metal and filling the designs with black inlay (line 20). Met’s niello glossary further describes a silver/copper/lead alloy with sulfur applied into an incised design and heated, then scraped to leave blackened compound in the incisions. Candidate has no distractor that asserts a particular copper/silver/sulfur recipe. Distinct from 098 enamel partitions and 099 fired enamel in carved cells.
sourceLocator: AAT 300054022 Note, line 20; corroborating Met “Seventeenth-Century European Watches,” Niello glossary definition
